React.memo cannot be applied to any component that internally uses a third-party charting library.
React.memo and code splitting are two different names for the exact same underlying mechanism, so either one would fix this equally well.
assessments.explanation: The problem described -- a slow initial load caused by a large library's JS having to be downloaded and parsed -- is a bundle-size problem, not a re-render problem, and memo has nothing to say about bundle size at all; it only ever decides whether to skip re-rendering a component that's already loaded and mounted. Reaching for memo here wouldn't reduce the amount of JS shipped or fetched on first load by even one byte. Code splitting via React.lazy and Suspense is the concept's actual tool for this specific problem, since it defers fetching that heavy component's code until it's genuinely needed, rather than bundling it into what every visitor downloads upfront regardless of whether they ever use it.

concepts.title: Deployment and Architecture
concepts.description: Most React apps ship through a build step into static assets with build-time environment configuration, benefit from a feature-based folder structure as they grow, and choose between client-side and server-side rendering as a genuine tradeoff rather than a default.
learningObjectives: Explain what the build step does to source code before it's deployed.
Explain how build-time environment variables configure the same codebase differently per environment, and their limits.
Contrast feature-based folder architecture with organizing by file type, and explain why the former scales better.
Explain the real tradeoffs between client-side rendering and server-side rendering.

sections.heading: The Build Step: From Source to Static Assets
sections.body:
Most React apps are not shipped as the JSX and modern JavaScript syntax actually written in the source files -- a build tool (Vite, webpack, and similar) runs a **build step** that bundles all of an app's JavaScript, CSS, and dependencies into a smaller number of optimized files; transpiles JSX and newer JavaScript syntax down into something every target browser can run; minifies the result (stripping whitespace, shortening variable names) to reduce file size; and often splits the output into multiple chunks, which is exactly the mechanism behind the lazy-loading pattern covered in the performance concept.

The output of this process is a folder of plain, static HTML/CSS/JS files, which get deployed to a server or CDN. 'Static' here means the server just hands these pre-built files out as-is on request -- it is not running any React code itself to produce them on the fly. That distinction matters later, when contrasted with server-side rendering, where a server does run React code on each request.

sections.heading: Environment-Specific Configuration
sections.body:
The same codebase typically needs to behave differently depending on where it's running -- pointing at `http://localhost:3000/api` locally, a staging server's URL in staging, and the real production API's URL in production. This is commonly handled with **build-time environment variables** -- `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` in Vite, or `process.env.REACT_APP_API_URL` in older Create React App setups -- which get substituted directly into the built JS files at build time, not read dynamically from the server's actual runtime environment the way a backend app's environment variables typically are. In practice, this means a distinct build generally needs to be produced per environment (or per deploy target), rather than one universal build deciding its own API URL by inspecting wherever it happens to be currently running.

There's a real security-adjacent point worth being explicit about: anything baked into a frontend build this way is visible to anyone who opens their browser's dev tools and looks at the shipped JS -- 'build-time environment variable' does not mean 'hidden' for a frontend app, the way it might for server-side configuration. This mechanism is appropriate for configuration (a base API URL, a public feature flag), never for secrets that genuinely need to stay private, like an API key that must not be exposed to end users.

sections.heading: Feature-Based Folder Architecture
sections.body:
As an app grows, how its files are organized starts to matter. Organizing by **file type** groups files into folders like `components/`, `hooks/`, `styles/`, each containing files belonging to every feature in the app, mixed together. Organizing by **feature** instead groups everything related to one feature together: `features/checkout/{CheckoutForm.jsx, useCheckout.js, checkout.css}`, `features/profile/{...}`, and so on.

The feature-based approach tends to scale better specifically because it makes the *relationships between files* explicit in the folder structure itself. In a type-based layout with, say, 200 components, the folder structure gives you no signal about which components belong to which feature, or which ones are safe to change or delete together -- that knowledge has to live entirely in people's heads or in scattered documentation. A `features/checkout/` folder tells you the likely blast radius of a change to checkout at a glance. This isn't a universal rule that every project needs from day one -- a small app with five components gains little from this ceremony -- it's a response to a specific growth problem, in the same spirit as when Context or a dedicated state-management library start earning their keep only once an app's state actually gets complex enough to need them.

sections.heading: CSR vs. SSR: A Brief, Honest Framing
sections.body:
Everything covered up to this point has assumed **client-side rendering (CSR)**: the server sends a nearly-empty HTML shell (commonly just `
`) plus a JS bundle, and the browser downloads and runs that JS, which then builds and inserts the actual UI. There's a real, measurable gap between 'the page arrives' and 'the page has visible content,' and a search engine crawler or a social-media link-preview bot that doesn't execute JavaScript may see nothing more than that empty shell. **Server-side rendering (SSR)** takes a different approach: the server itself runs the React components and sends back HTML that already contains real, visible content, so the browser has something meaningful to show immediately -- with the JS bundle still being sent and run afterward to 'hydrate' that markup, attaching event handlers and making it genuinely interactive. Each approach has real tradeoffs: CSR's upfront JS payload can mean slower time-to-first-visible-content, especially on slow connections or devices, but needs only simple infrastructure (a static file server or CDN is enough). SSR gives faster initial content and generally better default SEO and link-preview behavior, but requires an actual server running React on every request (or some pre-rendering/caching layer on top), rather than just handing out static files -- meaningfully more moving infrastructure to run and maintain. Next.js is the common way to get SSR (among other capabilities) in the React ecosystem, without needing to dive into its specific API here.

examples.title: The Same Source Code, Configured Differently Per Build
examples.explanation: The exact same line of source code, import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, resolves to a different literal string depending on which build was actually run -- the build tool substitutes the real value in at build time, baking it directly into the output JS file, rather than this being read dynamically from the server at request time the way a backend app's environment variable typically works. Running a production build with the wrong .env file active would silently point the deployed app at the wrong backend, with no runtime check anywhere catching the mismatch -- the value is fixed the moment the build runs, and stays that way until a new build is produced and deployed.

examples.title: Type-Based vs. Feature-Based Folder Structure
examples.code:
// Type-based (relationships between files are invisible in the structure):
src/
  components/
    CheckoutForm.jsx
    ProfileCard.jsx
    CheckoutSummary.jsx
    ProfileSettings.jsx
  hooks/
    useCheckout.js
    useProfile.js
  styles/
    checkout.css
    profile.css

// Feature-based (everything one feature needs lives together):
src/
  features/
    checkout/
      CheckoutForm.jsx
      CheckoutSummary.jsx
      useCheckout.js
      checkout.css
    profile/
      ProfileCard.jsx
      ProfileSettings.jsx
      useProfile.js
      profile.css
examples.explanation: In the type-based layout, everything related to checkout is scattered across three separate top-level folders that also happen to contain unrelated profile files sitting right alongside them -- deleting or substantially changing the checkout feature means touching, or at least checking, components/, hooks/, and styles/, and nothing about the folder structure itself signals that CheckoutForm.jsx and useCheckout.js are related at all. In the feature-based layout, that relationship is explicit in the structure itself: everything checkout needs lives inside features/checkout/, so a change or a deletion has an obvious, contained blast radius, and a new contributor can see at a glance what belongs together without cross-referencing several parallel folders.

misconceptions.description: Since API keys are read from environment variables and never appear as literal strings in the source code, they're safe to use as build-time env vars in a frontend app.
misconceptions.clarification: Anything baked into a frontend build via build-time environment variables ends up embedded inside the JS files the browser downloads and runs -- literally visible to anyone who opens browser dev tools and inspects the bundled source, regardless of how it was written in the original, un-built source code. Build-time env vars in a frontend app are appropriate for non-secret configuration (a base API URL, a public feature flag) that's genuinely fine for any user to see. Real secrets that must stay private belong on a server the frontend talks to over the network -- never baked directly into a frontend build.

misconceptions.description: Server-side rendering means React doesn't run in the browser at all for that page.
misconceptions.clarification: SSR generates the initial HTML on the server so there's real, visible content immediately, but the JS bundle is still sent to, and still runs in, the browser afterward -- a process called hydration -- to attach event handlers and make the already-rendered markup actually interactive. Without hydration, the page would look correct but nothing on it -- buttons, inputs, anything interactive -- would respond to user interaction. SSR changes where the first render happens and what the very first server response contains; it doesn't mean React never runs client-side at all for that page.

exercises.prompt: Your team's app has grown to 40 components, and finding all the files related to the 'notifications' feature currently means checking components/, hooks/, utils/, and styles/, since the app is organized by file type. What would reorganizing by feature look like for this specific case, and what problem would it solve?
hints: Identify every file across the current type-based folders that's actually about notifications, regardless of which folder it currently lives in.
A feature-based reorganization would gather all of those specific files into one place.
Think about what changes for someone who needs to modify, or safely delete, the notifications feature after this reorganization, compared to before.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Reorganizing by feature would mean creating a features/notifications/ folder and moving every notifications-related component, hook, utility, and style file currently scattered across components/, hooks/, utils/, and styles/ into that single folder together. This solves the exact problem described: instead of having to know (or discover, by searching) that notifications-related code exists across four separate, otherwise-unrelated top-level folders, everything the feature needs lives in one place. Someone modifying or safely removing the notifications feature afterward can see its full footprint at a glance, in one folder, rather than having to hunt through several parallel type-based folders and hope nothing related was missed.

exercises.prompt: A deployed production build is making API calls to http://localhost:3000/api, which obviously doesn't exist for real users. The code uses import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, and this worked fine locally. What's the most likely cause, and how would you actually fix it?
hints: Environment variables like VITE_API_URL are substituted in at build time, baked directly into the output files -- not read dynamically from whatever environment the running server happens to be in.
Consider which .env file (or equivalent build configuration) was actually active at the moment the production build was run for this deployment.

If the build was produced using a development env file, or no production-specific configuration existed at all, what value would VITE_API_URL end up baked in as -- and can that be fixed without a new build?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The most likely cause is that the production build was actually run with the development .env file active (or no distinct production env configuration existed at all), so VITE_API_URL got baked in as the localhost value at build time. Because that substitution happens once, at build time, and is fixed permanently into the resulting JS files, there is no way to fix this by editing a config file on the already-deployed server -- the wrong value is already embedded in the shipped bundle. The actual fix is ensuring a production-specific env file (or build configuration) with the correct API URL exists and is the one active when the build is produced for that deployment target, then rebuilding and redeploying an entirely new set of build artifacts -- editing anything after the fact on the running server has no effect on values that were already baked into the JS at build time.

assessments.prompt: A React app's production build makes a request to the wrong API URL because a build-time environment variable held the wrong value. Which statement correctly explains why this can't be fixed by just editing a config file on the already-deployed server?
options: Build-time environment variables like this are substituted directly into the JS bundle's literal source at build time, so the wrong value is already baked into the deployed files -- fixing it requires rebuilding with the correct value and redeploying the new build, not editing a file after the fact.
Frontend apps don't actually support environment-specific configuration at all.
The fix just requires restarting the static file server, which re-reads environment variables automatically on restart.
Environment variables in frontend builds are read fresh from the browser's own environment on every page load, so simply refreshing the page would fix it.
assessments.explanation: Build-time environment variables are substituted into the literal JS source at the moment the build runs, so the resulting value is permanently fixed inside the shipped files -- the only way to change it is to produce and deploy an entirely new build with the correct value active. Options B, C, and D each describe a mechanism that isn't how build-time environment variables actually work; none of them would have any effect on a value that's already baked into files that have already been built and deployed.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone deciding between a purely client-side-rendered React app and a server-side-rendered one, the real tradeoff involved -- not just 'SSR is better for SEO.'
assessments.modelAnswer: With client-side rendering, the server's initial response is a nearly empty HTML shell plus a JS bundle; the browser has to download and execute that JS before any real content appears, which creates a genuine gap between the page arriving and the page having visible content -- worse on slow connections or devices -- and a crawler or link-preview bot that doesn't execute JS may see only that empty shell, which is where the common SEO concern comes from. The upside is infrastructure simplicity: a static file server or CDN is sufficient, since nothing needs to run application code per request. With server-side rendering, the server itself runs the React components and sends back HTML that already contains real, visible content, so there's no gap between arrival and visible content, and crawlers see real content immediately without needing to execute JS at all. The cost is that an actual server (or an equivalent pre-rendering/caching layer) now needs to run React code on every request rather than just handing out static files -- meaningfully more infrastructure to run, scale, and maintain. Neither option is simply 'better' -- CSR trades initial content speed and default SEO behavior for infrastructure simplicity, and SSR trades that simplicity for faster initial content and better default SEO. Next.js is the most common way to get SSR (and related capabilities) within the React ecosystem, without needing to go into its specific API here.

assessments.prompt: An SSR page's initial HTML response already shows a fully-rendered product list. The instant the page appears, a user clicks "Add to Cart" on the first visible item -- but for a brief moment, nothing visibly happens. What's the most likely explanation?
options: SSR pages never support click handlers at all; only purely client-side-rendered apps can ever respond to click events.

The JS bundle needed to hydrate the page (attaching real event handlers to the already-rendered markup) may not have finished downloading and running yet -- the HTML looks complete and interactive, but nothing actually responds to events until hydration finishes.
The server has to fully re-render the entire page from scratch in response to every click, which explains the brief delay.
This indicates a bug specific to this app; a correctly built SSR page is otherwise always fully interactive the instant any content becomes visible.
assessments.explanation: SSR's server-rendered HTML gives the page real, visible content immediately, but that markup has no attached event handlers until the JS bundle sent alongside it actually finishes downloading and running -- the hydration step that attaches interactivity to already-rendered content. Until hydration completes, the page can look completely ready while still not responding to clicks, exactly the brief window described here; this is a normal, expected characteristic of SSR (sometimes felt as visible-but-not-yet-interactive), not evidence of a broken click handler or a per-click round trip to re-render the whole page server-side.
